title: Free vibration: the natural frequency of a mass bouncing on a spring
examples: How do I calculate natural frequency?
Why does a heavier mass vibrate more slowly?
What is the natural frequency of a car suspension?

explain.say: Push down on the corner of a car and let go: it bobs up and down at its own steady rhythm. Pluck a guitar string and it sings one note. Everything springy has a natural frequency, the rate it likes to vibrate when left alone. Here is the simplest model: a 2 kilogram mass on a spring.

draw.text: Spring stiffness k = 800 N/m, mass m = 2 kg

explain.say: Pull the mass down 10 millimetres and let go. The spring pulls it back, it overshoots, and it swings up and down forever, if nothing takes away energy. The graph shows a perfect sine wave, called simple harmonic motion. See it repeat? Count the waves in one second.

curves.label: Mass 2 kg
curves.ask: What does the sine curve show?

draw.text: Released from 10 mm below the rest position

explain.say: About three! The formula is omega n equals the square root of k over m: the square root of 800 over 2, which is 20 radians per second. Divide by 2 pi to get the frequency: about 3.18 hertz, so one bounce takes 0.314 seconds. See the dashed line at one period? What would a stiffer spring do?

curves.label: Mass 2 kg
curves.ask: What does the sine curve show?

explain.say: Make it faster! And a heavier mass makes it slower. Four times the mass, 8 kilograms, halves the frequency to about 1.59 hertz, because of the square root. Watch the new, slower curve. Notice the amplitude does not change the frequency at all. Does a big bounce take longer than a small one?

No, it takes the same time. Lovely! Handy trick: a spring that sags by delta under the weight has a natural frequency of one over 2 pi times the square root of g over delta. A car that sags 25 centimetres on its springs bounces at about 1 hertz, which feels comfortable. Challenge: what sag gives 2 hertz?

faq.q: What does the sine curve show?
faq.a: It shows the position of the mass against time. A pure sine wave means simple harmonic motion: the restoring force is proportional to the displacement.

faq.q: How does spring stiffness change the frequency?
faq.a: Natural frequency grows with the square root of stiffness. Four times the stiffness doubles the frequency.
asks: effect of stiffness on natural frequency

faq.q: Why does a heavier mass vibrate more slowly?
faq.a: More mass needs more time to speed up and slow down for the same spring force. The frequency goes as one over the square root of the mass.
asks: effect of mass on natural frequency

faq.q: How do I calculate natural frequency?
faq.a: Omega n equals the square root of k over m in radians per second. Divide by 2 pi for hertz. The period is one over the frequency.

faq.q: What is the natural frequency of a car suspension?
faq.a: Most passenger cars are tuned to about 1 to 1.5 hertz, close to the rhythm of walking, which people find comfortable.

facts: The natural frequency of an undamped spring-mass system is the square root of k over m, in radians per second.
For a linear spring, the natural frequency does not depend on the amplitude.

quiz.say: A 5 kilogram mass hangs on a spring of stiffness 500 newtons per metre. What is its natural angular frequency?
quiz.show: m = 5 kg on k = 500 N/m. Natural angular frequency ωn?

wrong.1: That is k over m without the square root.
wrong.2: That is the frequency in hertz, 10 over 2 pi, not in radians per second.

quiz.say: You double the amplitude of a spring-mass vibration. What happens to its period?
quiz.show: Double the amplitude of a spring-mass vibration. The period…
quiz.why: For a linear spring, the period depends only on m and k, not on amplitude.

wrong.1: The mass moves twice as far but also twice as fast, so the time is unchanged.
wrong.2: Amplitude does not change the period of a linear system.
